thread.title: Hidden Arbitrage In Covered Call Writing

author: Roy Haya
title: Hidden Arbitrage In Covered Call Writing
text:
Much of the feedback I received on my most recent article, "The Last Oil Arbitrage" was very positive with a hint of disappointment in that I only described the arbitrage after the opportunity had closed. As a follow up, the strategy described here is open to everyone, with a few conditions (of course).
Many investors use covered calls to enhance income, monetize volatility, and reshape the risk/reward profile of their long positions. This piece will not review covered call basics, but will describe a strategy that anyone could implement after the position is on.
Imagine transforming the economics of covered call writing from the traditional graph on the left as to that on the right Without Any Additional Risk:
(Source: Roy Haya)
This is possible by capitalizing on the interplay between short-term and long-term capital gains tax rates. As you may have guessed by now, the graphs above show the after-tax economics of covered call writing. The graph on the left shows the traditional economics of covered call writing, while the one on the right shows the after-tax economics of what can be described as the hidden possible arbitrage in covered call writing.
The conditions to achieve the economics of the graph on the right are listed below:
(Source: Roy Haya)
* If investor owned puts on the stock at the same time, the position becomes a tax straddle (IRC Sec. 1092), and opportunity can’t be exploited.
** According to IRC 1092 ( C ) (4), calls must have maturities greater than 30 days and less than 33 months; and strike price has to be greater than previous days close if less than 1 year assuming stock did not open 10% above prior day’s close. If longer than one year but less than 33 months, minimum call strike is previous day's closing price for the stock plus 2% per quarter increase to expiration. So a 13 month call would need to have a call strike greater than 8% out of the money.
If the underlying stock has been held for longer than 1 year, the call sold was out of the money when sold **, and there are short-term gains elsewhere in the year the trade expires, then this opportunity can be exploited. So instead of simply letting the call get assigned, the investor could simultaneously buy back the expiring call and sell the stock.
Covered Call Tax Basics
The gains and losses on covered calls are always short-term regardless of how long ago the call was sold, Unless the call is assigned against the long stock. Suppose a 13-month $110 strike call is sold against a stock trading at $100 for a premium of $10. If that call expires worthless, that gain is treated as short-term gain. If the call is exercised, that premium received adjusts the sale price of the stock. So if the stock was purchased at $80 and the call is assigned, the sale price for tax purposes will be the strike price plus the premium, or $120. Assuming the stock has been held for one year, that $40 gain is treated as a long-term gain. In effect, the call is ignored for tax purposes and the call premium received increases the gain on the stock.
In the example above, if the option was exercised when the stock was trading at $160, the investor would still be faced with a $40 long-term gain, and probably some remorse for having sold the call.
This need not be the case if the investor has short-term gains elsewhere in their portfolio. Instead of letting the call get assigned, suppose the call was unwound at the same time as the stock was sold (assuming there is no time value left). From a tax perspective, if the stock was trading at $160 at expiration, the investor would have an $80 ($160-$80) long-term gain and a $40 ($10 premium - $50 buyback) short-term loss. IF there are short-term gains elsewhere in the portfolio, the net effect converts $40 of short-term gains into $40 of long-term gains. In other words, the $40 of short-term loss created by this strategy offsets $40 of other short term gains elsewhere, leaving the investor with $80 of long-term gains (instead of $40 of long-term gains if the call is assigned and $40 of short-term gains elsewhere. So it’s possible to get more gain taxed at long-term rates, and create a short-term loss to use against short-term gains elsewhere in the portfolio.
Perhaps this might mitigate the call seller’s remorse.
FRICTIONS AND IMPLEMENTATION
Simultaneously buying a call and selling a stock as a spread order or paired trade is quite simple on many online option trading platforms. Executing in this manner removes the possible whipsaw of executing at slightly different prices of the underlying. In terms of frictions, assuming the option is very deep in the money with little to no time value, the investor may pay a few cents above intrinsic value to execute this trade. Additionally, there will be two commissions to pay instead of one for a call assignment. But the few cents of frictions may very well be worth it if the above fact pattern is in place.
It’s important to note that this should only be implemented if the call buyback results in a loss. In the above example, if the stock was at $115, buying back the call for a $5 gain and selling the stock produces a tax result that is worse than letting the call get assigned.
ASSIGNMENT ARBITRAGE FORMULA
Assuming the above conditions are met,
Arbitrage Benefit = (LOSS on Call Buyback) * (STCG – LTCG)
STCG=Short-Term Capital Gains Rate
LTCG=Long-Term Capital Gains Rate
Keeping with all of the aforementioned assumptions, the more the stock increases above the short call strike, the greater the benefit from this strategy.
CONCLUSION
Many investors that sell covered calls have likely seen their stocks called away over the last few years in names like AAPL, TSLA, AMZN, GOOG, NFLX, HLF, and MSFT, though recent volatility may have changed the current opportunity. Even ETFs like SPY, QQQ, and IWM (at various times) have seen dramatic increases. In situations such as these, this technique can potentially increase the after-tax return of call writing without altering the risk profile of the strategy at all. Further, the technique becomes more powerful the more the stock rises above the call strike. With technological advances and cost basis reporting by electronic trading platforms, it shouldn’t be much of a challenge to have these systems automatically flag such opportunities. From the standpoint of the investor, it means potentially significant tax savings. From the standpoint of the online trading system, it’s another commission. As long as there is a material difference between long-term and short-term capital gains rates, investors stand to gain from employing this technique.
